title: Expiring pages: data with a lifetime skips refresh entirely
idea: Po: memory that forgets on purpose. The allocator tags pages with a time-to-live (activations, gradients, KV of a finished request); the controller keeps a per-row TTL table, stops refreshing rows whose data expires or will be overwritten before the retention limit, and steers short-TTL data into weak-retention rows that would otherwise set the bank's refresh rate.
why: Refresh energy/bandwidth (fact 3): AI training buffers often live <100 ms, so 40-70% of rows in those regions skip refresh; weak-tail rows become usable instead of forcing repair, a few % yield.

title: Post-hammer neighbor de-trap pulse cancels injected charge
idea: Po: hammering heals the victim. After each aggressor precharge, the row decoder drives both adjacent wordlines ~0.3 V below the normal negative standby level for ~2 ns, sweeping carriers trapped or injected near the victim storage-node junction back to the substrate before they neutralize stored charge.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): attacks the trap-assisted electron-migration mechanism directly; claimed 5-10x higher flip threshold with no counter tables, at the cost of one extra negative-rail pulse per ACT.

title: Coset scrambling picks the least-coupled data pattern per row
idea: Po: memory that lies, but chooses its lie. On write, the controller tries four fixed scramble masks per row segment and stores the one minimizing charged-next-to-discharged adjacencies along bitline and passing-gate directions, recording the 2-bit mask ID in spare columns.
why: Data-pattern-dependent retention and coupling: the worst-case patterns that set the retention spec become rare, allowing ~1.5-2x longer refresh at ~0.4% capacity overhead.

title: Bit-plane transposition gives each bit significance its own refresh
idea: Po: low bits don't deserve to be remembered. The controller transposes bf16/fp8 tensors into bit planes in separate rows; sign/exponent planes refresh at 64 ms, upper mantissa at 256 ms, and the bottom three mantissa planes at 2 s or never (they are regenerated by the next training step).
why: Refresh (fact 3) for AI tensor regions: ~50-60% fewer refreshes; weak-tail rows can be assigned to LSB planes instead of being repaired.

title: On-die micro-heaters anneal leaky access transistors overnight
idea: Po: chips that heal while they sleep. A polysilicon heater grid under each mat pulses the local array to ~250-300 C for milliseconds during maintenance windows (data migrated out first), annealing interface and gate-oxide traps behind variable-retention-time and GIDL tail cells; the mat is re-profiled and returned to service.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3) and in-field aging: shrinks the VRT tail that forces worst-case refresh; claimed ~2x retention-tail improvement and recovery of degraded dies in the field.

title: Wafer-sibling weak-cell maps predict faults across a fleet
idea: Po: a die inherits its siblings' diseases. Every DIMM uploads in-field error and weak-row logs keyed by wafer lot and die (x,y); a fleet database learns spatial signatures such as edge-ring capacitor bowing and pushes predicted weak rows to sibling dies' controllers, which boost refresh on those rows or retire them before the first error.
why: Reliability without guard-band: vendors ship with less margin and hyperscalers cut uncorrectable errors by an estimated 30-50%, turning marginal dies into sellable parts.

title: Multi-reference soft sensing lets a 2 fF capacitor work
idea: Po: the capacitor is too small to matter. Each sense amp compares the bitline against three staggered references in one sensing window (time-multiplexed offset injection), emitting a hard bit plus a confidence flag; low-confidence bits go to the decoder as erasures, so cells with half the signal still read correctly.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): Cs can drop from ~5 fF to ~2-2.5 fF, so pillar AR falls from ~70:1 toward ~35:1 and the hardest etch steps go away.

title: Deliberately weakened canary cells set each subarray's refresh
idea: Po: memory that fails on purpose to warn you. Each subarray carries ~64 sentinel cells built with a thinned capacitor or an extra junction-leakage implant so they fail at ~0.6x the retention of the worst real cell; the in-DRAM scheduler slows refresh until canaries start to flip, then backs off one step.
why: Refresh (fact 3): each subarray runs at its true retention instead of the global worst case, ~2-4x fewer refreshes at normal temperatures.

title: Spectral activation listener detects hammer rhythms without row counters
idea: Po: the attacker sings, so listen for the song. A few Goertzel/sliding-DFT filters per bank analyze the time series of activated row-address bits; hammering shows up as sharp periodic peaks, which trigger targeted refresh of rows matching the peak's address hash, replacing large per-row counter tables.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) at ~1k thresholds, where counter SRAM becomes prohibitive: mitigation logic area down ~10x versus per-row counters.

title: Refresh-by-relocation: every refresh moves data to a new row
idea: Po: data runs away from the hammer. Instead of restoring a row in place, refresh copies it (RowClone-style, inside the subarray) to a free spare row and updates a small in-DRAM indirection table, so each logical row wanders across physical rows every window and no victim keeps the same neighbors for long.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): an aggressor's disturbance is spread over many short-lived residents; effective threshold x8-16 with ~1-2% spare rows.

title: Capacity-elastic twin-cell mode for deep sleep
idea: Po: memory that doubles itself to fall asleep. When a device idles, the controller compacts live data into half the rows and rewrites each bit into two cells on complementary bitlines; twin-cell differential sensing doubles signal, so self-refresh stretches from 64 ms to ~1 s.
why: Idle power (fact 3: refresh is 16-33% of idle): self-refresh power down ~10x during idle periods, at a temporary 2x capacity cost.

title: Leak-aligned inversion encoding keeps most cells discharged
idea: Po: memory that refuses to store ones. Retention errors only hit charged cells, so per 64-bit word the controller inverts the word (1 flag bit) whenever it would charge more than half the cells, respecting true-cell/anti-cell layout; sparse ML data then leaves only ~10-20% of cells charged.
why: Retention exposure (fact 3): halves or better the number of vulnerable cells, allowing ~1.5-2x longer refresh at ~1.5% overhead.

title: Compression-funded strong ECC lets marginal dies pass
idea: Po: ECC bits that cost nothing. The controller compresses each 64 B line (base-delta or zero-run); most real lines free 8+ bytes, which hold a strong BCH code, while incompressible lines fall back to standard SECDED and are steered to the strongest rows.
why: Yield: dies with higher weak-cell counts, previously scrapped, can ship, raising usable output ~5-10% with no extra ECC chips.

title: Organ-donor program: retired DIMMs reborn as a CXL cold tier
idea: Po: dead memory comes back to life. Hyperscalers route decommissioned DDR4/DDR5 through a retest line that builds per-die weak-row maps, then mount the modules behind CXL controllers with strong ECC and map-based row retirement as a cold memory tier for VMs and caches.
why: Supply: reuses millions of DIMMs a year; 10-20% of server capacity demand could be served by second-life parts at <30% of new-part cost during the shortage.

title: Move retention screening out of the fab and into boot
idea: Po: the factory never tests retention. Vendors skip the long multi-temperature retention test on ATE and ship with mandatory on-die BIST that profiles retention during first boots and idle periods, burning a weak-row map into antifuses and retiring or refresh-boosting rows in the field.
why: Capital (fact 4): retention test is a large share of tester time and capex; ~30-50% less ATE time, ~3-5% cost per bit, and a faster ramp.

title: Triple-row majority refresh votes critical data clean in-DRAM
idea: Po: the sense amp is the judge. Page tables, kernel text and model metadata are kept as three copies in one subarray; at refresh the DRAM does a triple-row activation whose charge sharing yields the bitwise majority, written back to all three rows, so scrubbing happens with no data movement.
why: Protecting the few critical bytes in-array lets the bulk of the device run looser refresh/ECC; scrub energy ~100x lower than reading out to the controller.

title: Buried electron-sink stripe between cells absorbs hammer carriers
idea: Po: rows have no neighbors. A shallow n-type collector stripe implanted between buried-wordline trenches and biased slightly positive captures electrons released by the aggressor's passing gate before they reach the victim storage-node junction.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) at the device level: claimed ~10x higher threshold; also trims junction-leakage coupling between adjacent cells.

title: Refresh-class die grades turn weak dies into discounted parts
idea: Po: sell the weakness. Dies that fail 64 ms retention but pass 32 ms or 16 ms are binned into refresh-class grades written into SPD; controllers read the grade and refresh those ranks faster, and the parts sell at a 20-30% discount for capacity tiers.
why: Usable supply: recovers dies now scrapped or downgraded, +3-8% bit output per wafer from a standards and business change alone.

title: Activation-rate billing makes row hammer an economic problem
idea: Po: hammering is legal but expensive. Cloud hypervisors meter each VM's per-row activation density from memory-controller counters, bill activation bursts beyond a budget, and throttle or live-migrate tenants whose activation pattern looks adversarial.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) in shared clouds: lowers reliance on costly in-DRAM mitigation, letting cheaper low-threshold dies be deployed safely.

title: Particle-strike detector strip triggers targeted neighborhood scrubs
idea: Po: memory that feels the bullet. A strip of deliberately charge-sensitive detector cells per bank records the time and position of alpha/neutron strikes; the controller at once scrubs only the rows in that strike's footprint, catching multi-bit clusters before a second hit makes them uncorrectable.
why: Soft errors: permits lighter per-line ECC because clustered multi-bit upsets are handled by locality, and cuts patrol-scrub bandwidth ~10x.

title: Pointer high-bit checksums catch flips without ECC chips
idea: Po: pointers that know where they should point. The compiler and runtime store a 12-16-bit checksum of each 48-bit pointer in its unused upper bits, checked on dereference by a cheap instruction; corrupted pointers trap and are reloaded from a replica.
why: Most catastrophic memory-error crashes are corrupted pointers; lets cheaper non-ECC DRAM serve more servers with crash rates closer to ECC parts.

title: Hammer-absorbing row cache intercepts repeated activations
idea: Po: the hammer hits a pillow. A small SRAM cache of 8-16 row buffers per bank inside the DRAM holds rows activated more than N times in a window; further ACTs to those rows are served from SRAM without raising the array wordline at all.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) and activation energy: attackers cannot toggle the hot wordline; also cuts ACT energy for hot rows ~30%.

title: Unidirectional codes exploit retention's one-way error direction
idea: Po: errors only fall downhill. Leakage only discharges cells (1->0 for true cells, 0->1 for anti cells), so the controller uses asymmetric Z-channel codes (a Berger-style count check plus a t-asymmetric BCH) laid out by cell polarity, correcting retention errors with fewer check bits than symmetric ECC.
why: Retention (fact 3): ~40% fewer check bits for the same retention coverage, or stronger correction that allows longer refresh.

title: Row-as-codeword: in-DRAM LDPC turns overfetch into redundancy
idea: Po: the 128x overfetch is a gift. Each 8 Kb row is one LDPC codeword (~10% parity) decoded by a parallel bit-flipping decoder at the row buffer on every activation, fixing the ~80 raw errors per row at 1% BER; the same decoder writes corrected data back during refresh so errors never accumulate.
why: Makes 1%-BER cells usable at ~10% overhead (Shannon floor at p=0.01 is ~8%) with ~10-15 ns decode added to tRCD; overfetch (fact 8) becomes useful work.

title: Stretch refresh until the raw error rate reaches 1%
idea: Po: memory that never refreshes on time. With 1% BER tolerated, the refresh window is set at the 1% quantile of the retention distribution (typically seconds) instead of the 64 ms dictated by the 1e-9 tail, and every refresh passes through the decoder as a scrub.
why: Refresh (fact 3): ~10-30x fewer refreshes, recovering 10-20% bandwidth and 15-30% of idle power at 32-64 Gb densities.

title: Self-assembled block-copolymer capacitor holes replace EUV layers
idea: Po: chips grown, not made. Capacitor hole arrays are patterned by directed self-assembly of a cylinder-forming block copolymer guided by a coarse DUV template; DSA's ~0.1-1% missing or merged holes, which kept it out of production, become dead cells that the code treats as erasures.
why: Capital/EUV (fact 4): removes 1-2 EUV layers (~5-10% wafer cost) while reaching ~10 nm-class hole pitch by self-assembly.

title: Halve the EUV dose; stochastic misprints become erasures
idea: Po: print the chip blurry. EUV dose on critical DRAM layers is cut 40-50%, raising scanner throughput ~1.5-1.8x, and the resulting rise in stochastic missing or bridged contacts (~0.1-1% of cells) is mapped at test as stuck cells, which as erasures cost about half the redundancy of random errors.
why: EUV chokepoint and capital (fact 4): the same scanner fleet patterns ~50% more wafer layers; ~5-8% lower cost per bit and less dependence on new scanners.

title: Unequal protection for KV caches: guard exponents, expose mantissas
idea: Po: memory that forgets the details but keeps the gist. LLM KV-cache tensors are split so sign and exponent bits sit in a strongly coded region while mantissa bits sit raw in 1%-BER cells; softmax averaging turns sparse mantissa flips into a negligible perplexity change.
why: KV cache is a fast-growing share of inference DRAM; ~70% of its bits move to cheap, rarely refreshed cells with ~2% total code overhead.

title: Low-Vt access transistors cut the wordline swing to 2 V
idea: Po: let the transistor leak. The access-transistor threshold is lowered ~0.3 V, so the wordline boost drops from ~3 V to ~2 V and the negative standby bias shrinks; the leakage tail grows until ~1% of cells fail retention within the window, which the code absorbs.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): wordline CV^2 energy down ~55%, smaller charge pumps (periphery, fact 7) and lower gate-oxide stress.

title: Diagonal codeword interleaving makes row hammer statistically harmless
idea: Po: let the rows flip. Each codeword's bits are spread diagonally across 16-32 physical rows in several subarrays, so a fully hammered victim row contributes at most 1/16 of any codeword's errors; with 1%-capable codes an attacker must flip dozens of bits in many rows at once.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): effective threshold x10-100 with no per-row counters; mitigation logic area largely removed.

title: Tiny unbalanced sense amps with offsets mapped as erasures
idea: Po: the sense amp is allowed to guess. Sense amplifiers are shrunk to minimum-size devices with no offset cancellation; the ~1% whose static offset exceeds the bitline signal are found at test and their columns treated by the decoder as known-position erasures.
why: Periphery (fact 7): sense-amp stripe area down ~30-40%, total die area down ~6-10%.

title: Four-level DRAM cells read with soft-decision decoding
idea: Po: one capacitor, two bits. Each cell stores one of four charge levels written by a stepped bitline driver and read by a successive-approximation sense; the ~1% level-confusion errors, Gray-coded so they are single-bit errors, are corrected by soft LDPC.
why: Density and cost per bit (facts 1, 4): ~1.8x bits per cell after code overhead without a lithography shrink.

title: Laser-crystallized poly-Si tiers for cheap 3D DRAM
idea: Po: build 3D DRAM from bad transistors. Each tier's lateral access transistors use excimer-laser-crystallized polysilicon (a display-industry process) whose grain-boundary variability gives a ~1% weak-cell tail; codewords span all tiers so a weak cell or even a poor tier is just an erasure.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2): a cheap deposited transistor that is good enough at 1% BER makes 26+ tiers plausible without epitaxial Si/SiGe stacks; ~2-3x lower cost per bit at 32+ tiers if it works.

title: DUV quad-patterning with a doubled overlay budget in mature fabs
idea: Po: make leading-edge memory in a trailing-edge fab. U.S. 28-40 nm-class fabs with immersion DUV run SAQP for the cell layers with overlay tolerances relaxed 2x; the resulting systematic misaligned contacts (~0.5-1% of cells) are mapped and corrected as erasures.
why: U.S. manufacturability and EUV independence (fact 4): ~16-18 nm-class cell density from existing U.S. tooling at roughly a third of an EUV DRAM fab's capex.

title: Delete repair: no spare rows, fuses, or laser repair
idea: Po: the chip arrives broken and that's fine. Redundant rows and columns, fuse banks, and the laser-repair and re-test steps are removed; every manufacturing defect up to 1% of cells is handled by the code as an erasure or error.
why: Periphery and test capital (facts 4, 7): ~3-5% die area and ~10-15% of test/repair cycle time removed.

title: Tungsten-free buried wordlines tolerate a slow far-end tail
idea: Po: wordlines with no tungsten. Buried wordlines use a TiN liner with heavily doped polysilicon fill instead of W; the higher RC under-drives far-end cells within the tRCD window, producing a ~1% incomplete-restore tail at mat edges that the code corrects.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%): removes the largest W use in the DRAM front end with no density loss.

title: Unsupported ultra-tall pillars: let 1% lean and short
idea: Po: let the capacitors fall over. Capacitor pillars are etched to AR ~115:1 without nitride support-mesh layers; the ~1% that lean, bridge or collapse become stuck cells mapped as erasures.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): reaches the higher Cs needed for scaling without a new dielectric, and removes 2-4 mesh deposition/patterning steps.

title: Hot-stacked DRAM bonded straight onto accelerators at 115 C
idea: Po: memory that loves the heat. DRAM dies are hybrid-bonded directly onto accelerator logic with no thermal derating; at 105-125 C leakage rises roughly 8-30x, and refresh is set so the hot-spot raw BER stays at or below 1%, which the code corrects.
why: Data movement (fact 5): logic-on-DRAM stacking cuts movement energy from 3-4 pJ/bit toward ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit and removes the thermal objection to it.

title: Double-length 1024-cell bitlines halve the sense-amp count
idea: Po: everyone shares one bitline. Bitlines grow from 512 to 1024 cells, halving the number of sense-amp stripes; the halved Cs/Cb transfer ratio raises sense errors to ~1%, which the code absorbs.
why: Periphery (fact 7): ~10-15% die area recovered.

title: Dirty-silicon DRAM grown in non-Spruce-Pine crucibles
idea: Po: memory made from dirty sand. Wafers come from ingots grown in synthetic-silica or lower-purity quartz crucibles, accepting more oxygen and trace metals; the extra generation-recombination centers fatten the junction-leakage tail to ~1% retention failures, which the code tolerates.
why: Scarce resource (Spruce Pine >80% of high-purity quartz): removes a single-point chokepoint and trims wafer cost ~5-10%.

title: Leaky rutile-TiO2 capacitors finally reach k near 80
idea: Po: a capacitor allowed to leak. Al-doped rutile TiO2 (k ~80-100) or SrTiO3 becomes the cell dielectric; it was rejected because its leakage tail breaks 64 ms retention, but with 1% BER tolerance that tail is acceptable.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): reaches the k ~70 target, keeping pillar AR at ~40-50:1 for the same Cs.

title: Iterative product codes with tiny hard-decision decoders
idea: Po: the code is a crossword puzzle. A 4 KB page is laid out as a 2D array protected by short BCH row and column component codes (like optical-transport staircase codes); a few rounds of iterative hard-decision decoding fix 1% BER at ~12-15% overhead.
why: Keeps 1%-BER memory affordable in power: ~10x less decoder energy than soft LDPC, well under 0.5 pJ/bit.

title: Writer-side stuck-at coding dodges defects instead of correcting them
idea: Po: the defects write the data. For stuck cells revealed by read-before-write, the encoder picks the coset of a partitioned linear code whose codeword matches the stuck values (Kuznetsov-Tsybakov defective-memory coding), so redundancy is about the defect fraction (~1%) rather than several times it.
why: Static 1% defects cost ~1-2% overhead instead of ~10%, so the defect tolerance itself costs ~5x less.

title: Panel-fab DRAM on Gen-8.5 glass with oxide-TFT access
idea: Po: memory printed like television screens. Idle flat-panel lines pattern 1T1C arrays on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass with oxide TFTs at sub-micron imprint rules; TFT variability gives ~1% BER, and the panels are diced into a near-DRAM capacity tier bonded to a logic decoder.
why: Capital: panel area costs ~100x less per m^2 than wafer area; ~$2-4/GB only if ~0.5 um rules are reached, with latency at the slow edge of DRAM-class (~100 ns+).

title: Flip-bounded number formats make weight memory ECC-free
idea: Po: numbers that can't be badly wrong. Weights use a redundant signed-digit encoding in which no single bit carries more than ~1/16 of the value range (e.g., 10 bits for 8-bit precision), so 1% raw flips act as small additive noise that noise-aware training absorbs with no decoder.
why: Zero decode latency and ~25% encoding overhead (vs ECC plus refresh) for the weight-streaming bulk of inference memory, run on cheap 1%-BER cells with minimal refresh.

title: Incremental-redundancy reads fetch extra parity only on failure
idea: Po: memory that talks like a cellular radio. Each line carries a short fast-path BCH; extra parity for a much stronger code sits in a separate row and is fetched HARQ-style only when the short decoder fails (a few % of reads at 1% BER).
why: Holds average access latency near the 10-100 ns DRAM class while guaranteeing 1%-BER correction; average latency penalty ~5-8%.
